name: AI Landscape
description: Interactive map of the AI tooling landscape: categories as systems, players in orbit.

categories.name: Foundation Models
categories.pls: Foundation models are the giant, general-purpose AI systems — trained on much of the internet — that everything else in the stack builds on; whoever has the best one sets the ceiling for every chatbot, agent, and copilot downstream. In mid-2026 the frontier is a three-way sprint between OpenAI (GPT-5.6), Anthropic (Claude), and Google (Gemini 3.x), with xAI close behind, while Chinese labs — DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax — flood the market with near-frontier open-weight models at commodity prices. Meta's pivot from open Llama to the closed Muse Spark shows how high the stakes have become.

players.name: OpenAI
players.pls: The company that started the modern AI boom with ChatGPT, still the most-used AI product on earth. Its GPT-5 line powers everything from consumer chat to enterprise agents. In July 2026 it made GPT-5.6 the new ChatGPT default, sold in three compute tiers (Luna, Terra, Sol) that let users trade cost against reasoning depth.

players.name: Anthropic
players.tagline: Claude models; enterprise and coding favorite
players.pls: The safety-focused lab behind Claude, now the enterprise and developer favorite — especially for coding and agent workloads. Its mid-2026 lineup pairs Claude Opus 4.8 with the newly released Sonnet 5 (June 30, 2026). Anthropic raised a $30 billion Series G at a $380 billion post-money valuation, one of the largest private rounds ever.

players.name: Google DeepMind
players.tagline: Gemini frontier models, everywhere Google is
players.pls: Google's consolidated AI lab ships the Gemini family — frontier models with the deepest product distribution on earth across Search, Android, and Workspace. Gemini 3.1 Pro leads accuracy benchmarks in mid-2026 (94.3% GPQA Diamond) with native Search grounding, and Google hedges both ways: its open-weight Gemma 4 models shipped in 2026 under a permissive Apache 2.0 license.

players.name: Meta
players.tagline: From open Llama to closed Muse Spark
players.pls: Meta's Superintelligence Labs stunned developers in April 2026 by releasing Muse Spark — its first closed, proprietary flagship — a retreat from the open-weight Llama strategy that once defined the company. Muse Spark is a natively multimodal reasoning model built for multi-agent orchestration; a paid Muse Spark 1.1 API followed in July 2026, Meta's first paid model.

players.name: xAI
players.tagline: Grok models and Grok Bot agents on X
players.pls: Elon Musk's lab builds Grok, the irreverent frontier model wired into X's real-time firehose and trained on the Colossus supercluster, shipping fast (Grok 4.5, July 2026). In August 2026 it pushed into "digital labor" with Grok Bot — always-on AI coworkers, each with their own cloud computer, that sign into your tools with your credentials and run multi-step jobs unsupervised.

players.name: DeepSeek
players.tagline: Open-weight frontier reasoning at cut prices
players.pls: The Chinese lab that shocked the industry in 2025 by matching frontier reasoning at a fraction of the training cost — and giving the weights away. Its 2026 flagship DeepSeek V4 ships as a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts 'Pro' plus an efficient 'Flash' variant, keeping relentless pressure on closed-model pricing worldwide.

players.name: Alibaba Qwen
players.pls: Alibaba's Qwen is the workhorse of the open-model world — among the most downloaded and fine-tuned families on Hugging Face, spanning tiny edge models to frontier scale. In 2026 it runs a dual track: continual open Qwen3.x releases alongside the proprietary Qwen 3.7 Max flagship, which posted a 97.1 on the HMMT February 2026 math benchmark.

players.name: Moonshot AI
players.tagline: Kimi: open models for agentic work
players.pls: Beijing-based Moonshot AI makes Kimi, the open-weight family that proved Chinese labs could lead on agentic and long-horizon tasks rather than just follow. Kimi K2 went viral for agentic coding in 2025; the 2026 Kimi K2.6 release was hailed by open-model trackers as 'one of the best open models out there yet again.'

players.name: Z.ai
players.tagline: GLM open models, coding-agent budget favorite
players.pls: Z.ai — the rebranded Zhipu AI, a Tsinghua spinoff — ships the GLM series, open-weight models that became a serious budget alternative inside coding agents. Its GLM-5 flagship and rapid GLM-5.1/5.2 updates in 2026 rank near the top of open-weight coding benchmarks while dramatically undercutting Western API prices.

players.name: Mistral AI
players.pls: Europe's flagship AI lab and the continent's answer to OpenAI, shipping open-weight models and enterprise platforms with a data-sovereignty pitch that resonates with EU governments and banks. In mid-2026 it was reportedly raising around €3 billion at a €20 billion-plus valuation — nearly double its prior mark — while expanding into robotics models and its own data centers.

players.name: MiniMax
players.tagline: Efficient open reasoning at commodity prices
players.pls: Shanghai's MiniMax jumped from consumer AI apps into the frontier conversation with its M-series of efficient open reasoning models. MiniMax M3, released June 1, 2026, scored 55 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at roughly $0.60 per million input tokens — near-flagship capability at commodity prices, typifying the Chinese open-weight cost squeeze.

players.name: Amazon
players.tagline: Nova models plus the Bedrock buffet
players.pls: Amazon's in-house Nova family gives AWS a first-party option alongside the third-party models (Anthropic, Mistral, Cohere) it hosts on Bedrock. Nova 2 foundation models landed in Amazon Bedrock in December 2025, positioning Amazon as the pragmatic enterprise choice: not frontier-leading, but inexpensive, multimodal, and wired into the world's biggest cloud.

players.name: Cohere
players.pls: Cohere is one of the few independent frontier labs, building models tuned for enterprise use: its Command family for generation, Embed for retrieval, and Rerank for search relevance. It emphasizes private, cloud-agnostic deployment for regulated industries, and its research arm Cohere Labs publishes open multilingual models like Aya.

categories.name: Coding Agents
categories.pls: Coding agents read whole repositories, plan changes, run tests, and ship working pull requests with light human supervision — a leap far beyond autocomplete. They are the breakout commercial success of the AI era, and developers were the first profession to reorganize daily work around them. By mid-2026 the terminal agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) rivals the AI-first IDE as the dominant form factor, labs increasingly pair agents with their own models, and consolidation is reshaping the field: Cognition owns Windsurf, Google folded Gemini CLI into Antigravity, and Sourcegraph spun Amp out on its own.

players.name: Claude Code
players.tagline: The terminal agent that set the standard
players.pls: Anthropic's terminal-native agent defined the agentic-coding form factor and became the benchmark other agents are measured against. It reads repos, runs commands, and orchestrates parallel sub-agents. Mid-2026 comparisons rank it the category leader, topping SWE-bench Verified at 88.6% with Claude Opus 4.8, on subscriptions running $20 to $200 a month.

players.name: OpenAI Codex
players.tagline: OpenAI's agent across CLI, IDE, cloud
players.pls: OpenAI's coding agent spans a CLI, IDE extension, and cloud sandboxes that run many tasks in parallel, bundled into ChatGPT subscriptions. Rebooted in 2025 as an agent (reviving the 2021 name), it led Terminal-Bench 2.0 at 82.7% in mid-2026 running GPT-5.5 codex models, making it Claude Code's closest rival.

players.name: Cursor
players.pls: Anysphere's AI-first editor became many developers' daily driver, blending chat, autocomplete, and background agents in a familiar VS Code-style shell. It reached roughly $2 billion in annualized revenue within three years, and by April 2026 was reportedly in talks to raise $2 billion-plus at a $50 billion valuation while in-house Composer models slash inference costs.

players.name: GitHub Copilot
players.tagline: The enterprise default AI pair programmer
players.pls: Microsoft's original AI pair programmer, now the enterprise default with over 20 million all-time users. It evolved from autocomplete into a full agent platform — you can assign GitHub issues to its autonomous coding agent — and went multi-model, routing across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models. At $10/month it remains the cheapest mainstream entry point.

players.name: Google Antigravity
players.tagline: Google's agent-first IDE and CLI platform
players.pls: Google's agent-first development platform, launched alongside Gemini 3 in late 2025, pairs an IDE with a mission-control surface for supervising fleets of agents. Google made it the center of its developer strategy in 2026, retiring the open-source Gemini CLI on June 18, 2026 and migrating users to the Antigravity CLI, free in public preview.

players.name: Windsurf
players.tagline: Agentic IDE, now part of Cognition
players.pls: The agentic IDE (formerly Codeium) at the center of 2025's wildest acquisition saga: OpenAI's ~$3 billion bid collapsed, Google hired away its CEO, and Cognition bought the company. Under Cognition it ships its own SWE-series coding models and in March 2026 scrapped its confusing credit system for straightforward quota-based plans.

players.name: Devin
players.pls: Cognition's 'AI software engineer' pioneered the fully autonomous agent you brief like a junior developer — it plans, codes, tests, and opens pull requests unattended. Once famously $500 a month, Devin's entry price fell to $20 with Devin 2.0, and Cognition — valued at $10.2 billion in its late-2025 raise — now pairs it with Windsurf's IDE.

players.name: Cline
players.pls: The leading open-source coding agent inside the editor — an Apache-2.0 extension for VS Code, JetBrains, and Neovim with over 5 million installs. Cline popularized transparent, approval-gated agent workflows and bring-your-own-model flexibility across 30+ providers, making it the default for teams that want agentic coding without vendor lock-in.

players.name: OpenCode
players.pls: A fast-growing open-source terminal agent from the SST team, pitched as the provider-agnostic Claude Code: one polished TUI, 75+ model providers, and multi-session parallel agents. It became a GitHub phenomenon, passing 160,000 stars by 2026 — a clear signal of developer appetite for agentic coding without lock-in.

players.name: Factory
players.tagline: Enterprise droids that ship whole tickets
players.pls: Factory builds 'Droids' — enterprise-grade autonomous software agents that work across CLI, IDE, Slack, and CI, designed to take whole tickets rather than assist keystrokes. A Terminal-Bench chart-topper in 2025, Factory raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.5 billion valuation in April 2026 to push agent-native development into large engineering orgs.

players.name: Amp
players.tagline: Frontier-only agentic coding, spun from Sourcegraph
players.pls: An 'unconstrained' agentic coding tool built by Sourcegraph's team and spun out as an independent company in 2026 to move faster. Amp targets power users: it always runs frontier models, supports sub-agents and an oracle reasoning mode, and its opinionated stances — no model picker, usage-based pricing — influence the whole category.

players.name: Jules
players.pls: Google's asynchronous coding agent: point it at a GitHub issue and it clones your repo into a cloud VM, writes the fix, and sends back a pull request. Out of beta since August 2025 and powered by Gemini, it stays notable for a generous free tier (15 tasks/day) and its fire-and-forget workflow.

categories.name: AI App Builders
categories.pls: Prompt-to-app (vibe-coding) platforms turn plain-English descriptions into working software — full-stack web and mobile apps with databases, auth, payments, and hosting — no programming required. They matter because they collapse the cost of building software toward zero and open development to non-engineers. Mid-2026's dynamic is hypergrowth plus a land grab: Lovable is reportedly in talks near a $13B valuation, Replit hit $9B, Emergent became a unicorn within a year, and incumbents Figma, Google, and Wix all ship competing builders, shifting the fight from cute demos to production-grade applications.

players.name: Lovable
players.tagline: Describe an app, get working software
players.pls: Stockholm-based leader of the vibe-coding wave: chat with an AI to build and ship full-stack web apps with auth, databases, and payments. One of the fastest-growing software companies ever, it raised $330M at a $6.6B valuation in December 2025 and by July 2026 was reportedly in talks to roughly double that.

players.name: Replit
players.tagline: Autonomous agent codes, tests, and deploys
players.pls: Cloud development platform whose Replit Agent turns prompts into deployed applications — Agent 3 added long-running autonomy and self-testing. Riding consumer and enterprise adoption of vibe coding, Replit raised $400M at a $9B valuation in 2026, tripling the $3B mark it set in September 2025.

players.name: v0 (Vercel)
players.pls: Vercel's generative builder turns prompts into polished React, Next.js, and Tailwind interfaces and full apps, deployable to Vercel in a click — the default choice when frontend quality matters. In 2025 it moved from v0.dev to v0.app as it grew into an agentic full-app builder, and Vercel opened v0's models to developers via API.

players.name: Bolt.new (StackBlitz)
players.pls: StackBlitz's builder runs an entire dev environment inside your browser tab via WebContainers, letting anyone prompt, edit, and deploy full-stack JavaScript apps. Its viral launch went from zero to roughly $40M ARR in about five months, driving a $105.5M Series B in January 2025, and it remains a staple of 2026 builder comparisons.

players.name: Base44 (Wix)
players.pls: Israeli platform famous for solo founder Maor Shlomo bootstrapping it to millions in profit before Wix acquired it for $80M in June 2025. Under Wix it became a surprise growth engine, reaching $100M ARR within nine months of the acquisition while targeting non-technical builders with built-in auth, databases, and hosting.

players.name: Figma Make
players.pls: Figma's AI builder turns prompts and existing design files into working prototypes and publishable web apps, keeping generation inside the design workflow teams already use. Launched at Config in May 2025 and rolled out to all full-seat customers, it anchored the AI story of Figma's July 2025 IPO year.

players.name: Firebase Studio (Google)
players.pls: Free, browser-based agentic development environment that superseded Project IDX at Google Cloud Next in April 2025 — prompt Gemini to scaffold full-stack apps wired into Firebase databases, auth, and hosting. It is Google's main answer to Lovable and Bolt, with App Prototyping agents that go from idea to deployed backend.

players.name: Emergent
players.pls: Indian-founded platform where autonomous agents plan, build, test, and deploy complete apps from a conversation, aimed squarely at entrepreneurs and SMBs. Users have created over 12 million apps, and in July 2026 Emergent became a unicorn, raising a $130M Series C at a $1.5B valuation roughly a year after public launch.

players.name: Anything (formerly Create)
players.tagline: Turn words into apps and businesses
players.pls: Startup previously known as Create (create.xyz) that rebranded to Anything, generating mobile and web apps, sites, and tools from plain text with integrated backends and payments. The rename accompanied a repositioning around building sellable products end-to-end, and 2026 reviews cover it as an active mid-tier rival to Lovable and Bolt.

players.name: a0.dev
players.pls: Y Combinator-backed builder focused on the mobile gap: it generates native iOS and Android apps with React Native from prompts, adding backend integration, payments, and one-click App Store and Google Play submission. The platform reports 200,000+ users and more than 300,000 apps created, making it the notable mobile-first specialist among 2026 builders.

players.name: Manus
players.pls: Manus is a general-purpose AI agent that plans and executes multi-step tasks end to end — researching, writing code, building sites, and producing finished deliverables from a single prompt. One of 2025-2026's most-discussed agent launches, it drew wide attention and a contested, ultimately abandoned acquisition saga, and is benchmarked against both autonomous agents and app builders.

players.name: Gamma
players.tagline: Prompt to decks, docs, and sites
players.pls: Gamma turns a prompt into polished presentations, documents, and websites, replacing slide-by-slide work with an AI-native canvas. With tens of millions of users and a multibillion-dollar valuation, it has expanded from decks into Gamma Sites and broader publishing, overlapping the prompt-to-app space while staying focused on visual, presentation-first output.

categories.name: Agent Frameworks & SDKs
categories.pls: Agent frameworks are the scaffolding for software that lets a language model plan, call tools, and work over many steps - handling state, retries, hand-offs between agents, and guardrails so developers don't rebuild that plumbing each time. By mid-2026 the field has consolidated: every major lab ships its own SDK (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, AWS), LangGraph and CrewAI anchor the open-source Python world, and TypeScript options like Mastra have gone mainstream. Differentiation has shifted from prompt-chaining to production concerns: durable execution, sandboxed code-running, memory, and interop standards like MCP and A2A.

players.name: LangGraph
players.pls: LangChain's low-level orchestration framework for building stateful, long-running agents as graphs, with checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, and streaming built in. It is the most widely deployed open-source agent framework, powering production agents at companies like Uber, LinkedIn, and JPMorgan; it reached v1.0 in October 2025 and passed roughly 35M monthly downloads by mid-2026.

players.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
players.pls: OpenAI's open-source SDK for building agents with handoffs, guardrails, sessions, and tracing. Successor to the experimental Swarm project, it became one of the fastest-adopted frameworks after its March 2025 launch. An April 2026 overhaul added a model-native harness plus built-in sandboxed code execution through providers like E2B, Modal, Daytona, and Cloudflare.

players.name: Claude Agent SDK
players.tagline: The agent harness behind Claude Code
players.pls: Anthropic's SDK exposing the same agent harness that runs Claude Code: an agentic loop with file tools, sandboxed shell, subagents, hooks, and native MCP support, in Python and TypeScript. Renamed from the Claude Code SDK in September 2025, it has become the default way to build Claude-powered agents that work directly with code, files, and computers.

players.name: CrewAI
players.pls: Open-source Python framework, and venture-backed company, for orchestrating role-playing agent 'crews' plus event-driven Flows, with a commercial enterprise platform on top. One of the most-starred agent projects at roughly 44k GitHub stars and about 5M monthly downloads in 2026, and the company claims adoption inside a majority of the Fortune 500.

players.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
players.pls: Microsoft's open-source .NET and Python framework merging AutoGen's multi-agent research lineage with Semantic Kernel's enterprise plumbing, wired into Azure AI Foundry. Announced in October 2025 and reaching general availability in 2026 - with an agent harness, hosted agents, and CodeAct shown at Build 2026 - it leaves standalone AutoGen and Semantic Kernel in maintenance mode.

players.name: Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)
players.pls: Google's open-source kit for building and orchestrating multi-agent systems in Python, Java, and Go, integrated with Gemini, Vertex AI Agent Engine, and the A2A agent-to-agent protocol. Launched at Cloud Next in April 2025, it powers Google's own Agentspace and passed roughly 3M monthly downloads within its first year.

players.name: Pydantic AI
players.tagline: Type-safe agents from the Pydantic team
players.pls: Python agent framework from the team behind Pydantic, bringing that library's validation-first, FastAPI-like ergonomics to agents: typed tools, structured outputs, dependency injection, and durable execution, with observability via Pydantic Logfire. It shipped a stability-committed v1.0 in September 2025 and is a favorite for regulated, schema-heavy production workloads.

players.name: Mastra
players.pls: Open-source TypeScript framework from the former Gatsby founders covering agents, durable workflows, RAG, memory, and evals - the JavaScript world's answer to LangGraph. It shipped v1.0 in January 2026 and raised a $22M Series A in April 2026 on top of a $13M seed, with users including Replit and SoftBank.

players.name: smolagents
players.pls: Hugging Face's deliberately tiny open-source agent library, around a thousand core lines, whose agents act by writing Python code rather than JSON tool calls and work with any model on the Hub or via APIs. Launched in late 2024, it powered Hugging Face's Open Deep Research demo in 2025 and remains the popular lightweight alternative to heavier frameworks.

players.name: Agno
players.pls: Open-source, full-stack Python framework, formerly Phidata, focused on fast and memory-efficient agent instantiation, multi-agent teams, and built-in knowledge, memory, and reasoning tools. In 2025 it rebranded from Phidata and shipped AgentOS, a self-hosted runtime and control plane with a UI for running agent fleets inside your own cloud.

players.name: Strands Agents
players.pls: AWS's open-source SDK taking a model-driven approach - give a model tools and a prompt and let it plan - with first-class MCP support and easy deployment to Lambda, Fargate, and Bedrock AgentCore. Open-sourced in May 2025 and at 1.0 since that July, it is used internally by Amazon Q Developer and AWS Glue.

players.name: Vercel AI SDK
players.pls: The Vercel AI SDK is a widely used open-source TypeScript library for building AI applications, offering a unified API across model providers plus streaming, tool calling, structured output, and UI hooks for React and other frameworks. Distinct from Vercel's v0 app generator and AI Gateway, it underpins a large share of production LLM apps in the JavaScript ecosystem.

categories.name: MCP & Tool Platforms
categories.pls: The Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, became the USB-C port connecting agents to tools and data - and a commercial layer grew around it: registries for discovering servers, platforms that host tools and manage OAuth, and routers that keep huge tool catalogs from overwhelming an agent's context. The defining mid-2026 dynamic is institutionalization: in December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, co-founded with OpenAI and Block; the November 2025 spec added async tasks, a July 2026 release candidate pushes stateless transport, and enterprise auth is the battleground.

players.name: Composio
players.tagline: Managed tools and auth for agents
players.pls: Integration platform giving agents authenticated access to 500+ apps like Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, handling OAuth and token management, with SDKs and hosted MCP servers. It raised a $25M Series A led by Lightspeed in July 2025 and launched Rube, a universal MCP server that routes agents to the right tools while avoiding context overload.

players.name: Zapier MCP
players.tagline: Thousands of apps, one MCP endpoint
players.pls: Zapier's MCP endpoint letting any agent or assistant call actions across the largest app catalog in automation, reusing Zapier's mature auth and permission controls. Launched in March 2025 with about 8,000 connected apps and 30,000+ actions, it advertises roughly 9,000 apps by 2026 and is often the fastest route to broad tool coverage.

players.name: FastMCP
players.tagline: The standard framework for MCP servers
players.pls: Pythonic open-source framework that made building MCP servers a few decorators' work; its 1.0 was folded into the official MCP Python SDK, while FastMCP 2.0 adds auth, proxying, composition, and testing. Creator Jeremiah Lowin (of Prefect) spun it into a company and launched FastMCP Cloud in 2025 for one-click hosted server deployment.

players.name: MCP Registry (official)
players.pls: The Model Context Protocol project's own open-source registry: a single canonical catalog of publicly available MCP servers with an API that downstream marketplaces and clients consume. Launched in preview in September 2025 and stewarded under the Agentic AI Foundation since MCP's December 2025 donation, it is turning ad-hoc server discovery into standardized infrastructure.

players.name: Smithery
players.tagline: Community registry and hosting for MCP
players.pls: One of the largest community marketplaces for MCP servers, where developers publish, discover, and one-click-deploy hosted tools for agents, with playgrounds and usage stats. Founded by Henry Mao, it became a default discovery hub during 2025's MCP boom and by 2026 lists thousands of servers spanning search, browsers, databases, and SaaS apps.

players.name: Pipedream
players.pls: Developer-focused integration and workflow platform whose Connect product exposes thousands of app APIs, with managed auth, as agent tools - including a hosted MCP server for every app in its catalog. Founded in 2019 and battle-tested by years of workflow automation, it pivoted hard into agent infrastructure in 2025, making MCP a first-class product line.

players.name: Arcade.dev
players.pls: Agent tool-calling platform built around user-scoped OAuth, so agents act as the actual end user in Gmail, Slack, or Salesforce rather than sharing service credentials. Founded by ex-Okta and ex-Redis engineers, it raised a $12M Series A in 2025, contributed to MCP's authorization spec work, and ships a managed runtime for deploying secure MCP servers.

players.name: Glama
players.pls: Independent hub that indexes and scores thousands of open-source MCP servers for quality and security, pairing its directory with an AI workspace and gateway for running tools across models. Built by developer Frank Fiegel, it became one of the most-trafficked MCP discovery sites through 2025-2026 and a common research stop before adopting a server.

players.name: Klavis AI
players.tagline: Hosted MCP integrations with Strata router
players.pls: Y Combinator-backed (X25) startup offering open-source and hosted MCP servers for a growing catalog of business apps with built-in OAuth, plus Strata, its router exposing one MCP endpoint that progressively reveals tools. Strata, launched in 2025, targets the context-overload problem that emerged as agent tool catalogs ballooned across the MCP ecosystem.

categories.name: Agent Memory
categories.pls: Agent memory layers give AI systems durable recall beyond a single context window: they extract facts from conversations and data, store them in vector indexes or knowledge graphs, resolve contradictions, and inject the right memories at the right moment. Good memory turns a stateless chatbot into an assistant that actually knows you, and it cuts token costs too. Mid-2026 dynamics: a funding wave led by Mem0's $24M raise, an architecture debate between graph-based and file-based memory - with Letta pivoting toward files - and growing pressure from model vendors building memory natively into their platforms.

players.name: Mem0
players.tagline: The memory layer for AI apps
players.pls: Open-source memory layer that extracts, consolidates, and retrieves facts from conversations so agents remember users across sessions, with a hosted platform and the OpenMemory local option. The category's community leader with tens of thousands of GitHub stars, it raised $24M across seed and Series A from Basis Set, YC, and Peak XV in October 2025.

players.name: Zep
players.pls: Agent memory platform built on Graphiti, its widely adopted open-source engine that assembles conversations and business data into a time-aware knowledge graph so agents can reason about how facts change. Zep published its temporal-graph architecture as a research paper in January 2025 and now positions itself as context engineering for enterprise agents.

players.name: Letta
players.pls: Agent platform from the UC Berkeley team behind MemGPT, the paper that introduced self-editing agent memory, treating memory blocks as first-class, transparent state. In March 2026 it refocused on Letta Code, an open-source, model-agnostic agent harness with persistent, git-backed 'context repositories' - a bet that agent memory belongs in files agents manage themselves.

players.name: LangMem
players.pls: LangChain's SDK for giving agents long-term memory: utilities that extract semantic, episodic, and procedural memories from conversations and store them in LangGraph's persistence layer, with background consolidation. Released in early 2025, it is the default memory choice inside the huge LangGraph ecosystem, though it remains a toolkit rather than a standalone hosted service.

players.name: Supermemory
players.tagline: Universal memory API for AI apps
players.pls: Hosted memory engine that ingests conversations, documents, and multimodal data and serves fast recall to any app via SDKs and an MCP connector. Built by young founder Dhravya Shah, it raised a $2.6M seed in late 2025 and has become a popular drop-in memory layer for consumer AI apps and assistant power users.

players.name: Cognee
players.pls: Open-source memory engine that replaces naive RAG by piping documents and interactions through an extract-cognify-load pipeline into a queryable knowledge graph plus vector store. Developer-focused and self-hostable with backends like Neo4j and Kuzu, it ranks among the most-cited open-source agent-memory frameworks in 2026 comparisons and roundups.

players.name: Memobase
players.pls: Open-source memory backend that maintains structured user profiles and event timelines rather than loose fact lists, aimed at companion, tutoring, and other user-centric apps that need to know who each user is. A lighter-weight newcomer, it appears across 2026 agent-memory roundups as the go-to option for profile-shaped memory, self-hosted or cloud.

players.name: MemMachine
players.pls: Open-source, self-hostable memory layer backed by infrastructure company MemVerge, exposing a model-agnostic API for capturing episodic, persona, and working memory across sessions and agents. Launched in 2025, it targets teams that want an Apache-licensed memory stack running on their own hardware instead of a hosted memory API, and features in 2026 memory-tool guides.

categories.name: LLM Gateways
categories.pls: LLM gateways sit between your app and the model providers: one API key, one bill, and automatic routing, fallbacks, caching, and spend controls across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and open models. As teams now routinely mix models, the gateway has become default plumbing for reliability and cost governance. The mid-2026 dynamic: OpenRouter hit a $1.3B valuation, platform vendors like Vercel and Cloudflare bundle gateways at zero markup, and ultra-fast open-source gateways (Helicone, Bifrost, TensorZero) are commoditizing the proxy itself, pushing commercial players up-stack into governance, guardrails, and observability.

players.name: OpenRouter
players.pls: A single API and marketplace routing requests across hundreds of models from dozens of providers, with unified billing, automatic fallbacks, and public usage rankings. Co-founded by OpenSea's Alex Atallah, it became the default way developers shop across frontier and open models. Raised a $113M Series B in May 2026 at a $1.3B valuation as token volume surged.

players.name: LiteLLM
players.pls: Open-source Python SDK and self-hosted proxy from BerriAI that puts 100+ LLM APIs behind one OpenAI-compatible interface, with virtual keys, budgets, caching, and fallbacks. It is the default self-hosted gateway for engineering teams, MIT-licensed and free to run, and still ranked best overall in multiple 2026 gateway comparisons.

players.name: Portkey
players.pls: Full-stack AI gateway combining routing to 1,600+ models with guardrails, prompt management, and governance controls, aimed at platform teams that need compliance (SOC 2 Type 2, HIPAA). Its core gateway is open source with a managed platform on top, and 2026 buyer's guides consistently rank it the strongest option for production guardrails.

players.name: Vercel AI Gateway
players.pls: Vercel's managed gateway gives one API key to hundreds of models with automatic failover, spend controls, observability, and BYOK, at zero markup over provider prices. Went GA in 2025 alongside AI SDK 5, and by 2026 added routing support for coding agents like Claude Code and Cline, pushing gateways toward free platform plumbing.

players.name: Cloudflare AI Gateway
players.tagline: AI traffic control at the edge
players.pls: Cloudflare's edge proxy adds caching, rate limiting, retries and fallbacks, logging, and cost visibility in front of any AI provider, with a free tier covering 100k logs per month. The zero-infrastructure choice for teams already on Cloudflare, and part of an AI cloud push capped by Cloudflare's late-2025 deal to acquire Replicate.

players.name: Kong AI Gateway
players.tagline: LLM traffic on enterprise API rails
players.pls: AI extension of Kong's widely deployed API gateway, adding multi-LLM routing, semantic caching and routing, prompt guardrails, and token-based rate limiting through familiar Kong plugins. The default path for enterprises that already govern APIs with Kong; 2026 comparisons rank it the top pick for API-management teams, with a free community edition and paid enterprise features.

players.name: Helicone AI Gateway
players.tagline: Rust gateway with observability built in
players.pls: YC-backed LLM observability company Helicone open-sourced a lightweight Rust AI gateway in 2025 that unifies major providers with logging, caching, and cost tracking in one hop. Its observability-first pitch: route and monitor together. Independent 2026 testing measured sub-5ms P95 gateway overhead at roughly 3,000 requests per second per instance.

players.name: TensorZero
players.tagline: Open-source gateway that learns from production
players.pls: Open-source Rust stack bundling an LLM gateway with observability, evals, experimentation, and optimization, a feedback loop that turns production data into better prompts and models. Apache 2.0 licensed, claiming sub-millisecond p99 gateway overhead at 10k+ QPS; raised a $7.3M seed led by FirstMark in early 2025 and gained strong GitHub traction since.

players.name: Bifrost (Maxim AI)
players.pls: High-performance open-source AI gateway written in Go by evals and observability company Maxim AI, claiming roughly 50x lower overhead than LiteLLM (under 100 microseconds at 5,000 RPS) with adaptive load balancing, cluster mode, guardrails, and 1,000+ model support. Launched in 2025, it is the newcomer pick when gateway latency itself is the bottleneck.

players.name: TrueFoundry
players.pls: Enterprise AI gateway and platform that deploys inside your own VPC, fronting 1,600+ models from 250+ providers with governance, cost controls, and rate limiting. Aimed at regulated enterprises that cannot route model traffic through third-party clouds; 2026 gateway buyer's guides rank it the strongest option for enterprise governance, with a free developer tier.

categories.name: Inference & Serving
categories.pls: This layer actually runs the models: hosted clouds serving open-weight models per token (Together, Fireworks, Baseten), custom-silicon providers selling raw speed (Groq, Cerebras, SambaNova), open-source engines powering most GPU serving (vLLM, SGLang), and local runtimes on laptops (Ollama, LM Studio). It matters because every app and agent pays this layer per token, and speed plus price decide what is buildable. The mid-2026 dynamic: agentic workloads sent demand vertical, with Cerebras pulling off 2026's biggest IPO, Baseten hitting $13B and Together $8.3B, while Cloudflare's acquisition of Replicate signaled consolidation.

players.name: Together AI
players.tagline: Cloud for open-model inference and training
players.pls: The leading independent cloud for open-weight models: serverless inference APIs, fine-tuning, and dedicated GPU clusters. Co-founded by Vipul Ved Prakash with Stanford researchers, it is a default home for Llama, DeepSeek, and Qwen workloads. Raised $800M at an $8.3B valuation in July 2026 as enterprise spend shifted toward open models.

players.name: Fireworks AI
players.tagline: Fast production inference for open models
players.pls: Speed-focused inference cloud founded by ex-Meta PyTorch leaders (CEO Lin Qiao), serving open models with heavy optimization, function calling, and fine-tuning for production apps. A default choice alongside Together for open-model APIs. Valued around $4B in 2025, and Bloomberg reported it in talks in May 2026 for new funding near a $15B valuation.

players.name: Groq
players.pls: Custom LPU chips deliver some of the fastest token generation available, sold through GroqCloud's OpenAI-compatible API with a popular free tier. Founded by TPU co-creator Jonathan Ross, Groq made raw speed the product. Raised $750M at a $6.9B valuation in September 2025, and 2026 benchmarks still rank its first-token latency among the best.

players.name: Cerebras
players.tagline: Wafer-scale chips, thousands of tokens per second
players.pls: Builds dinner-plate-sized wafer-scale processors that serve open models at extreme speed (about 3,000 tokens per second on gpt-oss-120B in 2026 comparisons), sold via API and enterprise systems. Went public on Nasdaq (CBRS) in May 2026, raising roughly $5.5B in the year's biggest tech IPO to date, with shares surging on debut.

players.name: SambaNova
players.tagline: Enterprise fast inference on RDU silicon
players.pls: AI chipmaker whose reconfigurable RDU processors power SambaNova Cloud, serving large open models at high speed for enterprises and governments. After 2025 layoffs it pivoted from training systems to focus squarely on inference. Raised roughly $1B at an $11B valuation in July 2026 as fast-inference demand accelerated.

players.name: Baseten
players.pls: Inference platform for companies running their own or fine-tuned models in production: optimized dedicated deployments, autoscaling, multi-cloud capacity management, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Popular with AI-native startups shipping mission-critical models. One of the fastest-rising infrastructure companies, raising a reported $1.5B Series F at a $13B valuation in June 2026, months after its $300M Series E.

players.name: Modal
players.pls: Serverless compute platform where you define GPU environments in Python and deploy inference, fine-tuning, or batch jobs that scale to zero with per-second billing. Beloved by AI startups (Suno runs on it) for making custom model serving feel like ordinary code. Reached a reported $1.1B valuation with its 2025 Series B.

players.name: DeepInfra
players.pls: No-frills hosted inference known for rock-bottom prices across one of the widest catalogs of open-weight frontier models, with an OpenAI-compatible API. A favorite budget backend behind routers like OpenRouter. In 2026 provider comparisons it is repeatedly the cheapest broad-catalog option, around $0.05 blended per million tokens on gpt-oss-120B.

players.name: vLLM
players.pls: The de facto standard open-source inference engine, born at UC Berkeley, whose PagedAttention memory management set the template for high-throughput LLM serving. Nearly every GPU inference provider runs vLLM or a fork of it. Became a PyTorch Foundation hosted project in 2025 and remains the default in 2026 engine benchmarks.

players.name: SGLang
players.tagline: LMSYS engine built for MoE serving
players.pls: Open-source serving engine from the LMSYS research team and vLLM's main rival, known for RadixAttention prefix caching and top performance on large mixture-of-experts models like DeepSeek. Joined the PyTorch ecosystem in 2025, and 2026 benchmarks show it trading wins with vLLM by workload, with structured output and agentic traffic among its strengths.

players.name: Ollama
players.tagline: Run models locally in one command
players.pls: The default way to run open models on your own machine: a free runtime with one-line model pulls, an OpenAI-compatible local API, and an official desktop app added in 2025. Massive developer adoption makes it the on-ramp for local AI. In late 2025 it added optional cloud-hosted models so the same CLI can offload models too big for a laptop.

players.name: LM Studio
players.tagline: Polished desktop app for local LLMs
players.pls: Desktop app from Element Labs for discovering, downloading, and chatting with local models on Mac, Windows, and Linux, with GPU offload, MLX support on Apple silicon, and a local OpenAI-compatible server. The GUI counterpart to Ollama for non-CLI users. Became free for work and commercial use in mid-2025.

players.name: NVIDIA
players.pls: NVIDIA makes the GPUs that train and run most of the world's AI, from Blackwell data-center chips to the CUDA software layer rivals struggle to displace. Its stack extends up through NIM inference microservices and DGX Cloud, and challengers like Groq, Cerebras, and SambaNova largely define themselves by how they try to beat it.

players.name: AMD
players.pls: AMD is the main challenger to NVIDIA in AI accelerators, with its Instinct MI-series GPUs and the open ROCm software stack. Backed by large deployments at hyperscalers and AI labs seeking supply diversity, it competes on memory capacity and price-performance while working to close the software-ecosystem gap that keeps NVIDIA dominant.

players.name: Hugging Face
players.pls: Hugging Face is the center of the open machine-learning ecosystem, hosting millions of models, datasets, and demo Spaces and maintaining core libraries like Transformers. Its Inference Endpoints and Providers run models in production, and for most researchers it is the default place to find, share, and deploy open models — including the protein and genomics models a life-sciences lab pulls down.

categories.name: Vector Databases
categories.pls: Vector databases store embeddings — the numeric fingerprints AI models use to represent meaning — and retrieve the most similar items in milliseconds, powering semantic search, recommendations, RAG, and agent memory. By mid-2026 the layer is consolidating: general-purpose databases (Postgres, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Redis) now bundle credible vector search, so specialists compete on scale, cost, and architecture — especially object-storage designs like Turbopuffer and LanceDB that slash costs at billion-vector scale. Agent memory and code retrieval for AI coding tools have become the hottest growth drivers, while category pioneer Pinecone changed CEOs amid intensifying competition.

players.name: Pinecone
players.pls: The startup that defined the managed vector-database category, offering serverless, fully hosted similarity search widely used for RAG and agent memory. In September 2025 founder Edo Liberty moved to chief scientist and veteran exec Ash Ashutosh became CEO; 2026 brought BYOC previews and new retrieval products (Nexus, KnowQL) as competition intensified.

players.name: Qdrant
players.pls: Open-source vector search engine written in Rust, prized for speed, rich filtering, and memory efficiency, with a managed cloud and strong adoption among AI startups. Berlin-based Qdrant raised a $50M Series B in March 2026 led by AVP, extending its push into enterprise hybrid search and agent-memory workloads.

players.name: Milvus / Zilliz
players.pls: LF AI & Data-graduated open-source vector database built for massive scale, with Zilliz selling the managed Zilliz Cloud. Deployments run past 100 billion vectors, and Zilliz claims its proprietary Cardinal engine delivers up to 10x higher query throughput than open-source HNSW setups — the heavyweight choice for enterprise-scale similarity search.

players.name: pgvector
players.pls: Open-source Postgres extension adding vector types with HNSW and IVFFlat indexes, letting teams keep embeddings next to relational data using plain SQL. Bundled by AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Supabase, and Neon, it is the pragmatic default at moderate scale — 2026 buyer guides consistently treat it as the cost baseline specialists must beat.

players.name: Weaviate
players.pls: Dutch-founded open-source vector database with hybrid search, built-in vectorization modules, multi-tenancy, and the managed Weaviate Cloud. A staple of enterprise RAG stacks, it restructured its cloud pricing in October 2025 around a new Flex tier while pushing agent-oriented tooling, keeping it among the most-deployed independent vector stores.

players.name: Chroma
players.pls: Open-source embedding database beloved for pip-install simplicity, making it the default for prototypes and AI-app tutorials since its $18M 2023 seed. Now repositioned as search infrastructure for AI, it launched Chroma Cloud, a usage-based managed service with Starter and Team ($250/month) tiers, moving beyond local-first roots toward production agent retrieval.

players.name: LanceDB
players.pls: Open-source, file-based vector database built on the Lance columnar format that runs straight off object storage like S3 — cheap, portable, and suited to multimodal data and training pipelines. A 2026 survey pegged it as the fastest-growing vector store by developer mindshare (6.7% to 9.6% year over year), alongside managed cloud and enterprise tiers.

players.name: Turbopuffer
players.pls: Serverless vector and full-text search built natively on object storage, cutting costs dramatically for huge, mostly-warm workloads. The quiet breakout of AI infrastructure: Sacra estimates it reached roughly $100M annualized revenue by March 2026, it powers search for Cursor, Notion, and Linear, and Thrive Capital invested in December 2025.

players.name: Vespa
players.pls: Yahoo-born search platform, spun out in 2023, combining vector, lexical, and structured retrieval with machine-learned ranking at extreme scale. In April 2025 Perplexity partnered with Vespa.ai to bring its web-scale search in-house on the platform — a flagship proof point for serving RAG over billions of documents with tensor-based ranking.

players.name: MongoDB Atlas Vector Search
players.tagline: Vector search in the document database
players.pls: Vector and hybrid search built into MongoDB Atlas, letting the huge Mongo install base add semantic retrieval without new infrastructure. MongoDB acquired embedding-model lab Voyage AI in February 2025 and now offers automated one-click embeddings inside Atlas — a bet that operational data and vectors belong in one platform.

players.name: Elasticsearch
players.pls: The dominant enterprise search engine now doubles as a vector database, pairing decades of BM25 lexical strength with dense-vector kNN and hybrid ranking. Elastic made its Better Binary Quantization compression generally available in 2025, sharply cutting vector memory use, and ELK-stack ubiquity makes it the default when teams already run Elastic.

players.name: Redis
players.pls: The ubiquitous in-memory data store extends into vector similarity, offering sub-millisecond retrieval for real-time RAG, semantic caching, and agent memory. Redis 8, released in 2025, introduced vector sets — a new native data type for embeddings — alongside its LangCache semantic-caching service, aiming squarely at low-latency AI workloads.

categories.name: RAG Frameworks
categories.pls: RAG frameworks wire retrieval into LLM applications: they ingest and index knowledge, fetch the most relevant context at query time, and ground model answers in your data rather than hallucination. By mid-2026 the category has moved past naive top-k vector lookup toward agentic retrieval — models that iteratively search, filter, and reason over knowledge bases — plus graph-based variants like GraphRAG and LightRAG. The big frameworks reached 1.0-era stability and monetize through commercial platforms (LangSmith, LlamaCloud), while managed services like Vectara sell the entire grounded-answer pipeline to enterprises.

players.name: LangChain
players.pls: The most widely adopted framework for building LLM apps, with retrieval chains, thousands of integrations, the LangGraph agent runtime, and LangSmith observability. LangChain and LangGraph hit 1.0 in October 2025, the same month the company raised a $125M Series B at a $1.25B valuation to build its agent engineering platform.

players.name: LlamaIndex
players.pls: The go-to open-source data framework for connecting LLMs to private data — loaders, indexes, and query engines — plus the commercial LlamaCloud for parsing and managed retrieval. With roughly 40k GitHub stars, it shipped LlamaCloud Index v2 in 2026 featuring agentic retrieval tools (retrieve, find, grep-style search) that go beyond top-k vector lookup.

players.name: Haystack
players.pls: Mature open-source framework from Berlin-based deepset for composable RAG and agent pipelines, known for production rigor and clean abstractions. At around 20k GitHub stars, it pairs with the commercial deepset AI Platform and visual deepset Studio, and remains a favorite for regulated European enterprises building search and question-answering systems.

players.name: RAGFlow
players.pls: Open-source RAG engine from InfiniFlow bundling the whole pipeline — deep document parsing, chunking, hybrid retrieval, grounded citations, and agent workflows — behind a polished UI. Its edge is extracting structure from messy PDFs and tables; with roughly 48k GitHub stars by 2026 it ranks among the most-starred RAG projects ever.

players.name: DSPy
players.pls: Stanford-born framework for programming LLM pipelines declaratively: developers specify modules and metrics, and DSPy compiles and optimizes prompts and weights automatically — popular for squeezing accuracy out of RAG systems. DSPy 3.0 shipped in 2025, and the project has grown to roughly 23k GitHub stars as prompt optimization went mainstream.

players.name: GraphRAG (Microsoft)
players.pls: Microsoft Research's open-source approach that builds a knowledge graph and community summaries over a corpus so LLMs can answer global questions spanning many documents. It ignited the graph-RAG wave; Microsoft's LazyGraphRAG variant defers LLM work to query time, cutting indexing costs to a tiny fraction while preserving comparable answer quality.

players.name: Vectara
players.pls: Managed RAG-as-a-service platform founded by ex-Google search veterans: upload data, get grounded answers with citations and hallucination scoring via its widely downloaded HHEM model. In April 2025 Vectara launched Open RAG Eval, an open-source framework for evaluating enterprise RAG quality, and it markets heavily to regulated industries.

players.name: LightRAG
players.pls: Open-source framework from University of Hong Kong researchers combining lightweight knowledge graphs with dual-level retrieval, delivering much of GraphRAG's quality at far lower cost and complexity. A breakout of 2025-26 with roughly 15k GitHub stars and published results outperforming several established RAG methods across evaluation dimensions.

players.name: txtai
players.pls: NeuML's open-source all-in-one framework: an embeddings database with combined vector and SQL-style search, RAG pipelines, and agent workflows in a single lightweight Python package. With over 10k GitHub stars, it appeals to teams wanting semantic search and RAG without stitching together separate vector stores, orchestrators, and servers.

players.name: R2R (SciPhi)
players.tagline: Production RAG engine with an API
players.pls: SciPhi's open-source RAG-to-Riches engine exposing a complete retrieval system — ingestion, hybrid and graph search, users and permissions — through a RESTful API. Holding around 6k GitHub stars, it added agentic reasoning and a Deep Research API that lets agents iteratively investigate knowledge bases, tracking the field's agentic turn.

players.name: Morphik
players.pls: Y Combinator-backed (2025) open-source RAG stack specializing in visually rich documents: it indexes pages as images with ColPali-style multi-vector embeddings so diagrams, tables, and schematics survive retrieval. A notable newcomer for technical-document Q&A, it offers a hosted service atop the open core plus knowledge-graph and cache-augmented techniques.

categories.name: Document Parsing & Ingestion
categories.pls: Every RAG or agent pipeline starts by turning PDFs, scans, spreadsheets, and slides into clean, structured, LLM-ready data — tables, layouts, handwriting and all. Parsing quality caps answer quality, which made this unglamorous layer one of 2025-26's hottest: vision-language models displaced classic OCR, frontier labs muscled in (Mistral shipped OCR 4 in June 2026), open-source converters like IBM's Docling and Datalab's Marker boomed, and investors poured money into accuracy-focused specialists — Reducto raised a $75M a16z-led Series B in October 2025 as enterprises race to unlock paperwork for agents.

players.name: Reducto
players.pls: San Francisco startup whose vision-first pipeline converts messy PDFs, scans, and spreadsheets into precise, LLM-ready structure, winning head-to-head accuracy bake-offs for finance, healthcare, and legal customers. Raised a $75M Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz in October 2025, bringing total funding to $108M — the best-funded parsing specialist.

players.name: LlamaParse (LlamaCloud)
players.pls: LlamaIndex's commercial parsing service tuned for RAG: it converts complex PDFs — tables, charts, multi-column layouts — into clean Markdown or JSON, with agentic modes that apply vision models to the hardest pages. It anchors LlamaCloud, whose 2026 Index v2 release added agentic retrieval over parsed documents, coupling ingestion tightly with retrieval.

players.name: Docling (IBM)
players.pls: IBM Research's open-source toolkit converting PDFs, Office files, and images into structured Markdown and JSON with strong table and layout understanding — free, local, and privacy-friendly. Donated to the Linux Foundation's LF AI & Data in 2025 and paired with IBM's compact Granite-Docling vision-language model (released September 2025) for end-to-end conversion.

players.name: Unstructured
players.pls: The company that made documents-to-LLM-ready-JSON a category, with open-source libraries embedded across the RAG ecosystem and an enterprise ETL platform with dozens of connectors. Still a default ingestion layer in 2026, it published a State of Generative Document Parsing white paper and public benchmarks claiming leading parsing quality.

players.name: Datalab (Marker)
players.pls: Brooklyn startup behind the hugely popular open-source Marker (PDF-to-Markdown) and Surya (OCR and layout) tools — together over 40k GitHub stars — plus a commercial API and on-prem licensing. Raised a $3.5M seed led by Pebblebed with Peak XV participating, and counts Anthropic as a confirmed customer of its small-model approach.

players.name: Mistral OCR
players.pls: Mistral AI's document-understanding model family offering fast, multilingual OCR that outputs structured Markdown with tables, math, and image grounding, via API or self-hosted on-premises. OCR 4, shipped in June 2026, added structure-aware extraction and bounding boxes — turning document parsing into a full enterprise play for the French frontier lab.

players.name: Extend
players.pls: New York startup building a full-stack platform for LLM-powered document processing — parsing, extraction, classification, human review, and evaluation tooling — so teams ship production document workflows quickly. Announced $17M in seed and Series A funding in June 2025 to build what it calls the document processing cloud.

players.name: Aryn
players.pls: Startup founded by database veterans offering DocParse for high-fidelity segmentation of complex documents and the open-source Sycamore engine for LLM-powered document ETL and analytics. Now positioned around agentic document intelligence, with a DataRobot integration that brings its document preparation into enterprise agent workflows.

players.name: Chunkr
players.pls: Open-source document intelligence API that parses PDFs, images, and spreadsheets into LLM-ready HTML, Markdown, or JSON — with OCR, layout detection, reading order, bounding boxes, citations, and schema-based extraction. Self-hostable with a hosted cloud option, it became a popular lightweight alternative to commercial parsers in 2025-26 RAG stacks.

players.name: LandingAI
players.pls: Andrew Ng's LandingAI pivoted from factory computer vision to document AI with Agentic Document Extraction (ADE), launched in 2025: vision models iteratively read complex documents and return structured fields with visual grounding for verification. Ng's developer reach gave ADE rapid uptake among teams parsing forms, tables, and charts.

categories.name: Web Scraping & Search APIs
categories.pls: These services fetch, clean, and structure live web content so AI systems can use it — crawlers and scraping APIs that turn messy pages into LLM-ready markdown or JSON, plus search engines built for agents rather than humans. They matter because models are frozen at training time; agents need fresh, grounded web data to be useful. In mid-2026 the layer is red-hot: Exa and Parallel raised at $2B+ valuations, proxy-era incumbents repositioned around MCP and agents, and search-for-agents has become its own funded market.

players.name: Firecrawl
players.tagline: Turns any website into LLM-ready data
players.pls: Open-source crawler and scraping API that converts websites into clean markdown or structured JSON for LLM pipelines and agents. YC-backed and hugely popular with AI developers, Firecrawl raised a $14.5M Series A in August 2025 alongside launching v2 of its API, and famously keeps a standing job offer for AI agents as employees.

players.name: Exa
players.tagline: The search engine built for AIs
players.pls: Neural search engine exposing embeddings-based web search, content retrieval, and deep-research APIs designed for models rather than people. A favorite backend for research agents, Exa raised a $250M Series C at a $2.2B valuation in May 2026 — one of the clearest signals that search for agents is now its own market.

players.name: Tavily
players.tagline: Web search API for AI agents
players.pls: Search-and-extract API purpose-built for LLM workflows, returning ranked, cleaned, citation-ready results agents can consume directly. It is the default search tool wired into many agent frameworks such as LangChain. Tavily raised a $25M Series A led by Insight Partners in August 2025 to power what it calls the internet of agents.

players.name: Parallel Web Systems
players.pls: Founded by former Twitter CEO Parag Agrawal, Parallel builds search, task, and extraction APIs made for AIs rather than humans, with accuracy-benchmarked deep-research endpoints. It hit a $2B valuation in April 2026 with a $100M Sequoia-led Series B, five months after its previous raise, making it the category's fastest riser.

players.name: Bright Data
players.tagline: Enterprise web data and proxy giant
players.pls: The largest web-data platform — proxies, scraping infrastructure, and datasets used by Fortune 500s and now AI labs. It won landmark US court rulings against Meta and X affirming the right to scrape public data, and in 2025 launched an AI-agent stack including a Web MCP server and Deep Lookup to feed live web data to LLMs.

players.name: Apify
players.pls: Prague-based full-stack scraping platform where developers publish and monetize Actors — prebuilt extractors for sites like TikTok, Amazon, and Google Maps. Long profitable and bootstrapped, Apify leaned into agents in 2025 with an MCP server that lets AI assistants discover and run any of its thousands of Actors as tools.

players.name: Zyte
players.pls: Formerly Scrapinghub, Zyte offers an all-in-one scraping API with automatic ban handling and AI-powered extraction, plus enterprise data services. It stewards Scrapy, the open-source Python scraping framework with 50,000+ GitHub stars, giving it deep credibility with developers now wiring web data into LLM and agent pipelines.

players.name: Jina AI (Reader)
players.pls: Berlin-based Jina AI's Reader converts any webpage into clean, LLM-friendly markdown just by prefixing the URL with r.jina.ai, alongside search and embeddings APIs. A generous free tier made it ubiquitous in RAG stacks, and Jina open-sourced ReaderLM-v2, a small specialized HTML-to-markdown model, in early 2025.

players.name: Brave Search API
players.tagline: Independent search index for AI grounding
players.pls: Brave's developer API exposes one of the only independent Western search indexes — tens of billions of pages built from real user visits rather than licensing Google or Bing, serving over a billion queries a month. That independence plus permissive AI-usage terms made it a standard grounding source for chatbots, RAG systems, and agent stacks.

players.name: Serper
players.tagline: Fast, cheap Google results as JSON
players.pls: Bootstrapped SERP API that returns Google results as structured JSON with sub-second latency at fractions of a cent per query. Its simplicity made it a go-to default inside open-source agent stacks and deep-research clones, and 2026 comparisons of agent search tooling consistently rank it among the cheapest and fastest options.

players.name: SerpApi
players.tagline: Structured results from every search engine
players.pls: The established SERP-scraping service: real-time structured JSON from Google, Bing, Amazon, YouTube, Maps, and dozens of other engines, with CAPTCHA solving and a Legal US Shield that indemnifies customers. Long a staple integration in LLM frameworks for giving models search results, it remains the most engine-complete option in 2026 roundups.

players.name: Linkup
players.tagline: Premium grounding search that pays publishers
players.pls: Paris-based search API for LLMs that licenses content from partner publishers and shares revenue with them, offering a legally cleaner grounding source for enterprise RAG. A notable European newcomer, Linkup claimed state-of-the-art factual accuracy on OpenAI's SimpleQA benchmark in 2025 and positions itself as the compliant alternative.

categories.name: Browser & Computer-Use Agents
categories.pls: This layer lets AI actually do things on the web — agents that click, type, fill forms, and complete tasks in real browsers, plus the infrastructure they run on: headless browser clouds, automation SDKs, and agentic browsers. It matters because most digital work happens in browsers with no API. Mid-2026's key dynamic is consolidation into the big assistants: OpenAI retired its Atlas browser and folded agentic browsing into ChatGPT, Google shipped Gemini auto-browsing in Chrome, Perplexity's Comet went free worldwide — while startups race to own the infrastructure layer and courts weigh agents' access rights.

players.name: Browser Use
players.pls: The most popular open-source framework for letting LLMs control real browsers — it extracts page structure so any model can click, type, and navigate. The YC-backed team raised a $17M seed in March 2025, and with 60,000+ GitHub stars it became the default DIY layer many commercial browser agents build on.

players.name: Browserbase
players.tagline: Headless browser cloud powering AI agents
players.pls: Infrastructure startup running fleets of stealth-capable headless Chrome sessions that agents rent by the second, plus Stagehand, its AI browser-automation SDK. Browserbase raised a $40M Series B at a $300M valuation in June 2025, then shipped Stagehand v3 in February 2026 — an AI-native rewrite it says is 44% faster.

players.name: Claude for Chrome (Anthropic)
players.tagline: Claude works inside your real browser
players.pls: Anthropic's extension puts Claude into Chrome to fill forms, manage email, and complete multi-step tasks under site-level permissions, building on the computer-use API Anthropic pioneered in 2024. Piloted with Max subscribers in August 2025, it expanded to Pro, Team, and Enterprise plans in December 2025 and added a faster Quick Mode in March 2026.

players.name: ChatGPT agent (OpenAI)
players.tagline: ChatGPT browses, clicks, and completes tasks
players.pls: OpenAI's computer-using agent lets ChatGPT operate a browser to research, shop, and finish work end-to-end — a lineage running from Operator (January 2025) through the Atlas browser (October 2025). In July 2026 OpenAI retired Atlas, setting an August 9 sunset and folding agentic browsing into the ChatGPT desktop app and a Chrome extension.

players.name: Perplexity Comet
players.pls: Perplexity's Chromium-based browser embeds an assistant that summarizes, compares, and acts across your tabs and logged-in accounts. Launched July 2025 and made free worldwide that October, its iOS app cracked the App Store top three in March 2026 — while an Amazon lawsuit over agent-driven shopping made Comet the test case for agent access rights.

players.name: Gemini in Chrome (Google)
players.tagline: Agentic browsing built into Chrome itself
players.pls: Google's push to make the world's default browser agentic: Gemini in Chrome answers across tabs, and an auto-browse agent descended from the Project Mariner research prototype shipped in January 2026 for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the US, with Google extending it to Android devices through 2026.

players.name: Dia (Atlassian)
players.pls: The Browser Company's successor to Arc, built around chatting with your tabs and reusable skills. Atlassian acquired the company for $610M in cash (announced September 2025, since completed) and is repositioning Dia as the AI browser for knowledge workers, wiring it into workplace context from tools like Jira and Confluence.

players.name: Skyvern
players.pls: Open-source, YC-backed platform that automates workflows on any website using vision-language models instead of fragile selectors — aimed at replacing RPA for jobs like invoice downloads and government filings. Skyvern 2.0 reported roughly 86% on the WebVoyager benchmark, state-of-the-art at its early-2025 release, and it remains a fixture of 2026 browser-agent roundups.

players.name: Hyperbrowser
players.tagline: Instant stealth browsers for AI agents
players.pls: Developer platform offering instant, scalable headless browser sessions with anti-bot stealth, CAPTCHA handling, and MCP support so agents and scrapers can browse reliably at scale. A newer entrant, it appears throughout 2026 field guides to browser infrastructure as one of the main alternatives to Browserbase for agent builders.

players.name: Steel
players.pls: Startup building an open-source browser-infrastructure layer: cloud Chromium sessions with session management, proxies, and anti-detection, callable through simple APIs or its self-hostable steel-browser project. Positioned as the transparent, open-core option in the stack, it features regularly in 2026 agent-tooling comparisons alongside Browserbase and Hyperbrowser.

players.name: Anchor Browser
players.tagline: Enterprise browser sessions for AI workflows
players.pls: Cloud browser platform pitched at enterprises: agents get isolated, authenticated sessions with credential management, proxy handling, and session recording for auditability, so automations can safely touch logged-in SaaS and internal tools. By 2026 it is prominent enough that rivals publish Anchor-alternatives roundups — a sign of real traction in the agent-infrastructure niche.

players.name: Kernel
players.tagline: Fast Chromium sandboxes for agent developers
players.pls: Y Combinator-backed infrastructure startup providing Chromium browser sandboxes that boot in milliseconds, with managed authentication, CAPTCHA handling, and replayable sessions for debugging agent runs. Kernel targets developers shipping web agents and deep-research products, and features in 2026 field guides to the emerging browser-harness stack.

categories.name: Observability & Evals
categories.pls: LLM apps and agents fail in ways normal software monitoring can't see, so this layer records every step a model or agent takes (tracing), scores outputs against test suites (evals), and tracks cost, latency, and quality in production. It's how teams ship AI with evidence instead of vibes. Mid-2026 is a consolidation-and-scale story: ClickHouse bought Langfuse, CoreWeave owns Weights & Biases, Braintrust hit an $800M valuation, and incumbents like Datadog muscled in — while OpenTelemetry-based tracing and agent-simulation testing became table stakes.

players.name: LangSmith
players.tagline: LangChain's platform for tracing and evals
players.pls: LangChain's commercial platform for tracing, evaluating, and monitoring LLM apps and agents, with deep LangGraph integration, prompt management, and self-hosted options. It's the default choice for the huge LangChain ecosystem but works framework-agnostically too. Parent LangChain raised $125M at a $1.25B valuation in October 2025, cementing LangSmith as the flagship of its agent-engineering stack.

players.name: Langfuse
players.tagline: Open-source LLM engineering platform, now ClickHouse-owned
players.pls: The most popular open-source LLM observability platform — tracing, evals, prompt management, and datasets — with 20,000+ GitHub stars and heavy self-host adoption in regulated industries. ClickHouse acquired Langfuse in January 2026; it stays MIT-licensed with Langfuse Cloud running as a standalone service. Enterprise users include Intuit, Twilio, and Merck, plus dozens of Fortune 500 companies.

players.name: Braintrust
players.pls: An eval-first AI engineering platform favored by top product teams like Stripe, Notion, and Airtable: experiments, dataset management, an LLM proxy, and agents that auto-improve prompts and evals. Braintrust raised an $80M Series B led by ICONIQ at an $800M valuation in February 2026, pitching itself as the observability layer for production AI.

players.name: Arize AI (Phoenix)
players.tagline: Enterprise AI observability plus open-source Phoenix
players.pls: Arize pairs an enterprise AI observability and evaluation platform with Phoenix, its OpenTelemetry-native open-source tracer that has passed 10,000 GitHub stars. With roots in ML model monitoring, it's strong among large enterprises running agents in production. Arize raised a $70M Series C in February 2025 and has leaned hard into agent evaluation and online evals.

players.name: Weights & Biases Weave
players.tagline: LLM tracing from the MLOps giant
players.pls: Weave extends Weights & Biases' widely used experiment-tracking platform to LLM applications: decorator-based tracing, evaluations, and production monitoring tightly coupled with W&B's training tools. Notable because millions of ML practitioners already live in W&B. CoreWeave completed its reported $1.7B acquisition of Weights & Biases in May 2025, folding Weave into its AI cloud.

players.name: Datadog LLM Observability
players.tagline: AI monitoring inside the observability incumbent
players.pls: Datadog's LLM and agent monitoring product brings tracing, quality checks, and cost tracking into the observability suite enterprises already run — one pane of glass for infrastructure and AI. It's the strongest incumbent pull on this category. In 2025 Datadog added LLM Experiments and agent monitoring, plus built-in hallucination detection and prompt-injection scanning.

players.name: Galileo
players.pls: An enterprise evaluation and observability platform whose research edge is Luna-2, small evaluation models that score outputs with sub-200ms latency — cheap enough to run as real-time guardrails. Customers include Twilio, Comcast, and HP. Galileo raised a $68M Series B in July 2025 and launched a free developer tier as it targets agent reliability.

players.name: Comet Opik
players.pls: Comet's open-source (Apache-2.0) platform for tracing, evaluating, and monitoring LLM apps and agents — the ML experiment-tracking company's second act. One of the fastest-growing tools in the space, Opik reached roughly 19,700 GitHub stars by mid-2026 and ships enterprise features like Kubernetes self-hosting alongside low-code integrations such as Dify and Flowise.

players.name: Helicone
players.pls: YC-backed open-source observability that starts as a one-line proxy: swap your base URL and get logging, caching, cost tracking, and automatic fallbacks across 100+ models. Popular with startups for near-zero setup. By 2026 Helicone had grown past 5,800 GitHub stars and evolved into a combined AI gateway and monitoring layer.

players.name: Confident AI (DeepEval)
players.pls: Confident AI is the cloud platform built on DeepEval, one of the most-used open-source LLM evaluation frameworks, offering 50+ research-backed metrics for RAG, chatbots, and agents in a pytest-style workflow. In 2025 it added red-teaming capabilities aligned to the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and NIST AI RMF, bridging evals and AI security.

players.name: Patronus AI
players.pls: Founded by ex-Meta AI researchers, Patronus builds automated evaluation and failure detection for LLM systems — known for its Lynx hallucination-detection model and Percival agent-debugging tool. In June 2026 it raised a $50M Series B and unveiled 'digital world models': simulated environments that stress-test AI agents before they touch real systems.

players.name: LangWatch
players.pls: Amsterdam-based, open-source (Apache-2.0) platform for agent simulation testing, evals, and observability, differentiated by EU data residency and ISO 27001 compliance for European enterprises like Backbase and PagBank. Through 2025-2026 it pushed into simulation-based agent QA, adding voice-agent simulations that rehearse realistic user scenarios before production deployment.

categories.name: AI Security
categories.pls: As companies wire LLMs and agents into real workflows, attackers target the AI itself: prompt injection, jailbreaks, poisoned models, data leakage, and hijacked agents holding real credentials. This layer supplies runtime guardrails, red-teaming, and posture management for AI fleets — research like EchoLeak, the zero-click Microsoft Copilot exploit, made the risk concrete. Mid-2026's defining dynamic is consolidation: Palo Alto (Protect AI), Check Point (Lakera), SentinelOne (Prompt Security), Cato (Aim), F5 (CalypsoAI), and Cisco (Robust Intelligence) all bought in, while independents like HiddenLayer, Noma, and Zenity race for the agent-security crown.

players.name: Palo Alto Prisma AIRS (Protect AI)
players.tagline: Palo Alto's end-to-end AI security platform
players.pls: Palo Alto Networks completed its acquisition of Protect AI in July 2025 and folded it into Prisma AIRS, a platform spanning model scanning, AI posture management, automated red-teaming, and runtime defense. Prisma AIRS 2.0, launched October 2025, added agent security plus integrations with ServiceNow, IBM, and Glean — the benchmark for big-vendor consolidation.

players.name: Lakera (Check Point)
players.pls: Zurich-founded Lakera made prompt-injection defense mainstream with Lakera Guard, a real-time firewall for LLM apps, and Gandalf, the viral jailbreak game whose millions of attack attempts trained its detection models. Check Point acquired Lakera in a reported $300M deal announced September 2025, making it the core of Check Point's end-to-end AI security stack.

players.name: HiddenLayer
players.tagline: Independent security for models and agents
players.pls: The most prominent still-independent AI security pure-play: model scanning, AI detection and response, red-teaming, and — since March 2026 — agentic runtime protection. Strong in government and defense, it was named an awardee on a US Missile Defense Agency contract vehicle in December 2025 and struck 2026 partnerships with Databricks and Cohere.

players.name: Cisco AI Defense (Robust Intelligence)
players.tagline: AI security fused into Cisco's network
players.pls: Cisco's AI security suite, built on its 2024 acquisition of red-teaming pioneer Robust Intelligence. Launched in January 2025, it pairs automated model vulnerability testing with network-enforced runtime guardrails for AI apps and agents, feeding Cisco's broader security cloud — the clearest example of AI security merging into core infrastructure.

players.name: Prompt Security (SentinelOne)
players.tagline: GenAI usage and app protection, SentinelOne-owned
players.pls: Israeli startup securing both employee GenAI use (shadow AI, data leakage) and homegrown LLM apps against prompt injection and jailbreaks. SentinelOne acquired it for $250M in August 2025 — just two years after founding — to anchor its AI security strategy, extending Prompt's protections across SentinelOne's endpoint and cloud platform.

players.name: Aim Security (Cato Networks)
players.pls: Aim's researchers discovered EchoLeak, the first zero-click AI vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot (June 2025), proving agents can be silently hijacked via a crafted email. The Israeli company secures employee AI use and in-house AI apps; SASE vendor Cato Networks acquired it in September 2025 to build AI security into its cloud network.

players.name: Noma Security
players.tagline: End-to-end platform for AI agent security
players.pls: Independent platform covering the full AI lifecycle: discovery of every model and agent (AI-SPM), supply-chain scanning, red-teaming, and runtime threat detection, pitched at Fortune 500 teams consolidating point tools. Noma raised a $100M Series B in 2025 — among the largest AI-security rounds ever — to chase the agent-security land grab.

players.name: Zenity
players.tagline: Security and governance for AI agents
players.pls: Agent-security specialist protecting enterprise copilots and low-code agents — Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude, OpenAI AgentKit, custom builds — with buildtime governance and runtime defense. Its Zenity Labs research disclosed AgentFlayer, zero-click agent-hijacking attacks revealed at Black Hat 2025, and the company made the 2026 Fortune Cyber 60 as agent governance went board-level.

players.name: F5 AI Guardrails (CalypsoAI)
players.pls: F5 acquired CalypsoAI for $180M in 2025 and relaunched its technology as F5 AI Guardrails and F5 AI Red Team in October 2025. CalypsoAI's model-agnostic inference protection and adaptive agentic red-teaming now ship inside F5's application delivery and security platform, putting AI guardrails in front of the large enterprises F5 already serves.

players.name: Guardrails AI
players.pls: The best-known open-source framework for wrapping LLMs with programmable input/output validators, plus the Guardrails Hub library of prebuilt checks for PII, hallucinations, and toxicity. Founded by Shreya Rajpal, it's taught in a DeepLearning.AI course with Andrew Ng. In 2025 it launched Snowglobe, a simulation product generating synthetic conversations to test chatbots pre-launch.

players.name: Gray Swan AI
